1.title: AI, ML and Deep Learning: Core Concepts
1.text: Welcome to Module one: A I, M L and Deep Learning: Core Concepts. This module covers task statement one point one, and it gives you the vocabulary that every other module builds on. You will learn what A I, machine learning and deep learning are, how they relate, and how training, inference, data and learning types fit in. You will also meet fit, bias, large language models, generative A I and agentic A I.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Define the basic terms: A I, M L, deep learning, neural network, model, algorithm, training and inference. Name the fields of A I: computer vision, N L P and speech recognition. Tell the types of inference, the types of data and the types of learning apart. Explain bias, fairness and fit. And separate L L Ms, generative A I and agentic A I from the rest.

1.title: Case Check-In: Cedar and Salt Hears the Buzzwords
1.text: At Cedar and Salt Travel, the leaders keep saying A I, M L, Gen A I and agents, as if they were one thing. The product team wants a shared vocabulary before it picks any tool. The first question is simple: what is each term, and how do they relate? Your job is to give the team clear definitions, and a way to tell them apart.

1.title: How AI, ML and Deep Learning Fit Together
1.text: Start with how the big terms fit together. The figure shows nested boxes. Artificial intelligence is technology that lets machines do human-like problem-solving tasks. Machine learning is a branch of A I that learns from data instead of following explicit instructions. Deep learning is machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers. And generative A I is an advanced form of deep learning that creates new content. Not all A I is machine learning, because A I is the umbrella term. Exam tip: nesting from the outside in goes A I, then M L, then deep learning, then generative A I.

1.title: Machine Learning, Models and Algorithms
1.text: Machine learning analyzes data without explicit instructions. It learns patterns from examples. An algorithm is the method that learns from the data. A model is the result: the learned patterns, stored in its parameters. Training is the learning step, and the model is then tested on data it has not seen. A trained model takes new input and gives an output, such as a prediction. Exam tip: the algorithm is the recipe, and the model is what the recipe produces after training.

1.title: Neural Networks and Deep Learning
1.text: A neural network is inspired by the human brain. It is made of many connected artificial neurons, arranged in an input layer, one or more hidden layers and an output layer. Deep learning uses networks with many layers. It can process unstructured data, such as images, speech and text, without manual feature extraction. The price is that it needs a lot of data and a lot of computing power. Exam tip: the word deep in deep learning means many layers.

1.title: The Fields of AI: Vision, Language and Speech
1.text: A I has several fields, and the exam expects you to match a task to its field. Computer vision extracts information from images and video, like spotting a damaged room in a photo. Natural language processing, or N L P, interprets and understands human language in text, like finding the sentiment of a review. Speech recognition turns spoken words into text and finds meaning, like transcribing a customer call. Machine translation, named-entity recognition and sentiment analysis are N L P tasks. Recommendations, fraud detection and forecasting are other common uses. Exam tip: pictures mean computer vision, written language means N L P, and spoken words to text means speech recognition.

1.title: Training and Inference
1.text: Two words appear everywhere: training and inference. The figure shows the flow. In training, the model learns from data, and it takes time and compute. In inference, the trained model is used on new input to give a prediction or an answer. Training happens before use. Inference happens every time the model is used. That is why most of the ongoing cost of a live application is inference. Exam tip: training builds the model, and inference uses it.

1.title: Types of Inference
1.text: There are four types of inference to know. Real-time inference uses an always-on endpoint that answers each request quickly, and it fits interactive, low-latency needs. Serverless inference needs no infrastructure to manage and scales with traffic, so it fits idle periods between bursts, as long as cold starts are acceptable. Asynchronous inference queues requests and processes them later, and it fits large payloads, up to one gigabyte, and long processing, up to one hour. Batch inference runs the model over a whole dataset, and it fits when no persistent endpoint is needed. As of the fifth of November, twenty twenty-six, the limits come from the Amazon SageMaker A I documentation. Exam tip: instant answers mean real-time; a whole dataset with no endpoint means batch; large or slow requests mean asynchronous.

1.title: Types of Data
1.text: Next, the types of data. Labeled data has the right answer attached to each example, such as reviews tagged positive or negative. Unlabeled data has examples without answers. Structured or tabular data has rows and columns in a fixed layout, like a bookings table. Time-series data records values over time, like daily bookings. And unstructured data has no fixed layout: text, images, audio and video, like photos and call recordings. Exam tip: labeled data has answers, and structured data has a fixed layout. They are different questions, so do not mix them up.

1.title: Types of Learning
1.text: There are three types of learning to know. Supervised learning learns from labeled data and predicts a known kind of answer, a category or a number. Unsupervised learning learns from unlabeled data and finds patterns or groups by itself. Reinforcement learning learns from rewards for its actions and finds the best sequence of steps toward a goal. Semi-supervised learning mixes a little labeled data with a lot of unlabeled data, though it goes beyond the guide. Remember: supervised covers classification and regression, unsupervised covers clustering, and reinforcement uses a reward and a goal. Exam tip: labels given means supervised, no labels means unsupervised, and a reward signal means reinforcement.

1.title: Design Check: Cedar and Salt's First Vocabulary
1.text: Now a design check. Cover the right column and answer each row yourself. Reading a guest review to find the sentiment: N L P. Spotting a damaged room in a photo: computer vision. Transcribing a recorded call: speech recognition. Scoring tonight's bookings with no endpoint running: batch inference. Grouping guests into segments with no labels: unsupervised learning. And predicting cancellations from past labeled bookings: supervised learning. Pause the video if you want more time.

2.title: Fit: Underfitting, Overfitting and a Good Fit
2.text: Now fit. The figure shows three cards. Underfitting means the model is too simple. It does poorly on the training data and on new data, and it has high bias. A good fit captures the main pattern and works on new data too. Overfitting means the model memorizes the training data and fails on new data, and it has high variance. To fix underfitting, use a more capable model or better features. To fix overfitting, use more data or a simpler model. Exam tip: great on training data but poor on new data means overfitting.

2.title: Bias and Fairness
2.text: Bias in A I is a systematic error that favors or harms some outcomes or some groups. It often comes from unrepresentative data, or from choices in the model. Fairness means the system treats different groups equitably. Biased data can make biased predictions, even when the model is accurate overall. Module eleven covers bias and fairness in depth. Exam tip: biased data in means biased predictions out.

2.title: Large Language Models and Generative AI
2.text: Generative A I creates new content: text, images, audio, video and code. A foundation model, or F M, is trained on broad, unlabeled data and handles many tasks. A large language model, or L L M, is a very large deep learning model pre-trained on huge amounts of text. Most L L Ms use the transformer design and have billions of parameters. An L L M predicts the next token, which lets it write, summarize, translate and answer questions. Exam tip: every L L M is a foundation model for language, and a foundation model is a form of generative A I.

2.title: Agentic AI
2.text: Agentic A I is an autonomous A I system that acts independently to reach pre-set goals. It is goal-driven: it plans steps, uses tools and adapts as new information arrives. It keeps memory, so long tasks stay consistent. Ordinary software follows fixed rules, and an assistant that only answers a prompt is not yet agentic. Modules four and seven cover how agents are built. Exam tip: autonomy, goals, tools and memory are the signs of agentic A I.

2.title: Telling Them Apart
2.text: Here is a table to tell the terms apart. A I is machines doing human-like problem solving; the key word is umbrella. M L is A I that learns from data; the key word is patterns. Deep learning is M L with many-layer neural networks; the key word is layers. Generative A I is deep learning that creates content; the key words are new content. And agentic A I is A I that acts toward goals with tools; the key word is autonomy. Exam tip: pick the key word in the question: umbrella, patterns, layers, new content or autonomy.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: Core Concepts
2.text: Here is how the exam frames this module. Which term: A I, M L, deep learning, Gen A I or agentic A I, from a short description. Which field: computer vision, N L P or speech recognition. Which inference: real-time, serverless, asynchronous or batch. Which data: labeled or unlabeled, structured or unstructured, or time-series. Which learning: supervised, unsupervised or reinforcement. And which problem: underfitting, overfitting or bias. Exam tip: name the situation first, then the term.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Nesting: A I, M L, deep learning and generative A I, with agentic A I acting toward goals. An algorithm trained on data produces a model: training builds it and inference uses it. Inference comes in four types: real-time, serverless, asynchronous and batch. Data can be labeled or not, and structured or not, and learning can be supervised, unsupervised or reinforcement. Underfitting is high bias, and overfitting is high variance. And L L Ms are huge deep learning models trained on text that predict the next token.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Which statement correctly describes how A I, machine learning and deep learning relate? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Machine learning is a branch of A I, and deep learning is machine learning with many-layer neural networks. A I is the umbrella, machine learning learns from data, and deep learning uses networks with many layers. The other options reverse or confuse the relationship.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Cedar and Salt wants to score last month's bookings for cancellation risk in one overnight job, and it does not want an endpoint left running. Which type of inference fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B, batch inference. It runs a model over a whole dataset without a persistent endpoint. Real-time and serverless inference serve individual requests as they arrive, and asynchronous inference queues large or slow individual requests.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Select two. Which two of these are examples of unstructured data? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and C. Photos and call recordings have no fixed row-and-column layout, so they are unstructured. Tables, spreadsheets and database rows are structured or tabular data.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. A model scores very well on its training data but poorly on new bookings. What is the most likely problem? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D, overfitting, with high variance. A model that memorizes its training data but fails on new data is overfitting. Underfitting would do poorly on both the training data and new data.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Cedar and Salt builds an assistant that sets its own steps toward a booking goal, uses tools such as search and payment, and remembers the traveler's earlier choices. Which term describes it best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A, agentic A I. Autonomy, goals, tool use and memory are its signs. Computer vision works on images, unsupervised learning finds patterns in unlabeled data, and batch inference runs a model over a dataset.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. The team groups guests into segments by behavior, and none of the guests has a label. Which type of learning is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C, unsupervised learning. Finding groups in data without labels is usually clustering. Supervised learning needs labeled examples, and reinforcement learning learns from rewards for actions.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all six answers. Question one: A. Question two: B. Question three: A and C. Question four: D. Question five: A. Question six: C. That completes Module one. Next, Module two covers practical use cases for A I, how to choose the right technique, and the A W S services that handle common A I tasks.
